To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) there are no significant differences in the use of the verb-noun collocations between the three groups of participants, (b) the participants’ use of the verb and noun collocations is similar to that of the native speakers, (c) the participants’ performance on the verb and noun tests was not significantly different.
the verb-noun collocation is the most frequently used lexical unit in journalistic prose and that it is also the most productive, in the sense that the number of new collocations is increasing.

(1) the verb-noun collocations in journalistic prose are largely drawn from a small set of familiar, well-established, and widely known patterns; and (2) these patterns are often used in a way that suggests that they are already moribund or even dead.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature and extent of lexical patterning, and its implications for the way in which we teach and learn vocabulary.

the extent to which the language of newspapers is ‘lexicalized’ in the sense that it draws heavily on established collocations and idioms, and to what extent it is ‘open’ in the sense of using new combinations of words that are not yet fixed in the language.
the extent to which the language of the news media reflects the linguistic knowledge and communicative competence of the general public.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the language of journalism, at least in the quality press, is a highly conventionalised and conservative variety of English, in which the most striking lexical feature is a heavy reliance on familiar and well-established collocations, and in which the incidence of idioms is low, and of neologisms virtually non-existent.
the language of news reporting is a language of formulae, a language of clichés.
the lexical patterning of news prose is highly conservative, and that the most frequent collocations in the genre are the most familiar ones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more we learn the language, the more we can understand the language.
the use of collocations is not a matter of choice but rather a matter of necessity.
we have been able to show that the use of collocations is a common feature of journalistic language.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are a number of ways in which we can use the internet as a tool for language learning.
, for the most parts, collocations are not the result of a writer’s creativity but are a product of the language’s historical evolution.
